linkedin:
A QR code is usually a black-and-white grid nobody looks at twice — and once it's printed, the destination it points to is fixed for good. QRON generates QR codes as actual artwork through an image-generation pipeline, while keeping them scannable, and each code is Ed25519-signed and anchored under the AuthiChain protocol so its authenticity can be verified at scan time instead of just assumed.

The part worth noticing isn't the art — it's that the destination behind a QRON code can be updated after the code is already printed. A product label, a poster, or a business card doesn't need to be reprinted when what it should point to changes; the code stays put, the "Living Portal" behind it doesn't have to.

If you're printing static links onto physical products or packaging today and reprinting every time the destination changes, take a look at how a signed, editable QR code works.

reddit.title: QR codes usually can't change where they point after they're printed. This one can.
reddit.body:
QRON generates QR codes as actual artwork — run through an image-generation pipeline so the code doesn't look like a plain black-and-white grid — while staying scannable. Each code is Ed25519-signed and anchored under the AuthiChain protocol, so a scan can verify the code's authenticity instead of just trusting whatever URL happens to be embedded.

The part I think is actually useful: the destination behind a QRON code (a "Living Portal") can be updated after the code is printed. The code on the label, poster, or card stays the same — only what it resolves to changes, so a changed destination doesn't force a reprint.

Curious if others here have run into the reprint-on-change problem with static QR codes on physical products or marketing materials, and how you've worked around it.

Disclosure: I work on this project.
